meta.title: Who really said "Do what you can, with what you have, where you are"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Theodore Roosevelt wrote it — but credited it to Squire Bill Widener of Virginia in his 1913 Autobiography, and the real wording is "with what you've got."
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Do what you can, with what you have, where you are'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Roosevelt's own line: in his 1913 Autobiography he credited it to Squire Bill Widener of Widener's Valley, Virginia — and wrote "you've got," not "you have."

answer.label: Not Theodore Roosevelt — quoted from Squire Bill Widener
answer.authorDates: Farmer of Widener's Valley, Virginia; life dates unknown · quoted by Roosevelt in 1913
answer.sourceLine: Roosevelt did write these words — but in his 1913 Autobiography he explicitly credited them to Squire Bill Widener of Widener’s Valley, Virginia, and his recorded wording was ‘with what you’ve got,’ not ‘with what you have.’ The popular version drops both the true source and the original phrasing.

source.heading: Roosevelt’s Autobiography — crediting Squire Bill Widener

Squire Bill Widener, Widener’s Valley, Virginia

source.excerpt: There is a bit of homely philosophy, quoted by Squire Bill Widener, of Widener’s Valley, Virginia, which sums up one’s duty in life: ‘Do what you can, with what you’ve got, where you are.’
trail: In his 1913 Autobiography (Ch. IX), Roosevelt introduces the line as “homely philosophy, quoted by Squire Bill Widener.”
The Theodore Roosevelt Center confirms Roosevelt credits Widener, not himself.
The Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library lists it among misquotes — wrong source and “have” for “you’ve got.”
Quote Investigator traces the wording and the family of related sayings back to Roosevelt’s 1913 record of Widener.
source.cutTag: ↑ Roosevelt names the true source in the same sentence — and writes ‘you’ve got,’ not ‘you have’
source.excerptNote: The widely shared version silently strips the attribution to Widener and smooths “you’ve got” into “you have,” leaving a line that reads as Roosevelt’s own maxim.

author.name: Squire Bill Widener
author.heading: About Squire Bill Widener
author.metaLine: fl. early 1900s · farmer, Widener's Valley, Virginia
author.bio: Squire Bill Widener was a farmer of Widener’s Valley in southwestern Virginia, otherwise unrecorded by history. He owes his one line of fame to Theodore Roosevelt, who in his 1913 Autobiography quoted Widener’s “homely philosophy” — “Do what you can, with what you’ve got, where you are” — as a summary of one’s duty in life. Because Roosevelt was famous and Widener was not, the saying was gradually re-credited to the President, erasing the man who supplied it.

copyAttribution: Squire Bill Widener, quoted in Theodore Roosevelt's "An Autobiography" (1913): "Do what you can, with what you've got, where you are." — often misattributed to Roosevelt himself.

misattribution.heading: How Roosevelt got the credit
misattribution.intro: Roosevelt is the reason the line survives — but he never claimed it. He set it down as a saying he was quoting, and named the man he heard it from in the very same sentence.

items.why: The line does appear in Roosevelt’s 1913 Autobiography, but he frames it as “homely philosophy, quoted by Squire Bill Widener” — not his own words. The TR Presidential Library lists the popular Roosevelt attribution among its misquotes.

items.who: Arthur Ashe (“Start where you are, use what you have, do what you can”)
items.why: A closely related motivational rewording — “Start where you are, use what you have, do what you can” — circulates under Arthur Ashe’s name; it is a separate later phrasing, not Roosevelt’s or Widener’s original.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are Squire Bill Widener’s; Roosevelt was the messenger who wrote them down and, unintentionally, lent them his name — see the Theodore Roosevelt Center.

context.heading: A saying that outran its source
lead: The phrase is one of the most-shared “Roosevelt” quotes on the internet, printed on posters, mugs, and graduation cards. Its appeal is its plainness: make do, start now, don’t wait for better circumstances.
That plainness is exactly why it drifted. Roosevelt presented it as folk wisdom — and folk wisdom, once attached to a famous name, tends to stay there.
detailsBody: Roosevelt’s recorded text reads “with what you’ve got.” The dominant modern version substitutes “with what you have,” a small smoothing that, together with the dropped attribution, converts a quoted rustic saying into a presidential aphorism.
context.pull: Roosevelt wrote it down; Widener said it first.
